title: Sixty-One Per Cent of Asian Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Already Show Early Muscle Loss. South Asians Are the Most Vulnerable Group. Your Parents May Not Know They Have It.
excerpt: A new meta-analysis of 14 studies across Asia found that sarcopenia begins years before diabetes patients notice it — and the vegetarian diets many Indian families follow may be accelerating the decline.
body:
Your parents call it getting old. Their doctor, if they have one, calls it aging. The clinical term is sarcopenia — the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength that begins silently in midlife and accelerates with every passing decade. For most people, it is invisible until a fall, a fracture, or a sudden inability to climb stairs forces a reckoning.

For South Asians with type 2 diabetes, that reckoning may come earlier than anyone expects.

## The Numbers Are Worse Than You Think

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the *Journal of Diabetes Investigation* in January 2026 — covering 14 studies and thousands of Asian adults with type 2 diabetes — found that 61 per cent already showed signs of early sarcopenia. When measured using DXA scans (the gold standard), the prevalence reached nearly 30 per cent for confirmed sarcopenia. Using bioelectrical impedance, a less precise but more accessible method, the number was around 20 per cent.

A separate 2025 study found that 30 per cent of geriatric patients with type 2 diabetes had full-blown sarcopenia, and 27 per cent had frailty — a condition that drastically increases the risk of hospitalisation and death.

The link between diabetes and muscle loss is not coincidental. High blood sugar damages the molecular pathways that regulate muscle protein synthesis. Insulin resistance — the hallmark of type 2 diabetes — impairs the body's ability to build and repair muscle tissue. Over time, the muscles waste while the fat around them accumulates, creating a condition called sarcopenic obesity that is particularly dangerous and particularly difficult to detect in people who appear to be a normal weight.

## Why South Asians Are Uniquely Vulnerable

South Asians develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMIs, at younger ages, and at higher rates than almost every other ethnic group on the planet. A Harvard-led study recently confirmed that the standard BMI threshold of 25 misses millions of South Asians who should be screened at 20. The combination of earlier diabetes onset and longer disease duration means the muscle-wasting process has more years to progress undetected.

There is another factor that rarely makes it into the medical literature but is glaringly obvious to anyone who has eaten in an Indian household: protein intake.

The traditional Indian vegetarian diet — built around dal, roti, rice, sabzi, and yogurt — is nutritionally rich in many respects. But it is chronically low in protein by modern clinical standards. The recommended daily intake for preserving muscle mass in older adults is 1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. Most Indian vegetarians consume between 0.6 and 0.8 grams. That is roughly half of what their muscles need.

A 12-week study published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* found that elderly women who consumed 1.2 grams per kilogram per day showed significant improvements in muscle mass and grip strength compared to those eating normal amounts. The difference was measurable on MRI scans.

Your mother's dal has protein. It does not have enough.

## The Intermittent Fasting Problem

The fastest-growing dietary trend among Indian tech workers in the United States — and increasingly among their parents back home — is intermittent fasting. The 16:8 protocol (eating only within an eight-hour window) has been promoted as a weight loss strategy, a metabolic reset, and even a longevity hack.

For people already struggling with insufficient protein, it may be making things worse.

A muscle-centric review published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* argued that intermittent fasting reduces the postprandial amino acid availability that muscles need to repair and grow. The compressed eating window means fewer opportunities to distribute protein across the day — and protein distribution matters. Muscles can only absorb and use about 25 to 40 grams of protein per meal. Cramming a day's worth into two meals does not produce the same result as spreading it across three or four.

A Korean study of adults found that higher meal frequency — three or more meals per day — was independently associated with lower odds of low muscle mass, even after adjusting for total protein intake.

The irony is sharp. Many Indian Americans adopt intermittent fasting to improve their metabolic health. But if they are already protein-deficient and beginning to lose muscle mass, the fasting protocol may be accelerating the very decline they are trying to prevent.

## What Sarcopenia Actually Costs

This is not an abstract concern. A meta-analysis of 15 studies found that sarcopenia in type 2 diabetes patients increases all-cause mortality by 72 per cent (hazard ratio 1.72), cardiovascular disease risk by 94 per cent (HR 1.94), and the odds of diabetic complications — including neuropathy, retinopathy, and kidney disease — by 149 per cent (odds ratio 2.49).

For NRI families, the practical implications are immediate. Your parents in India may have diabetes that is managed with medication and diet. But if no one is testing their muscle mass, grip strength, or walking speed, the sarcopenia progressing underneath may be the greater threat to their independence and survival.

## What You Can Do — Starting This Week

The evidence is clear on what works, and none of it requires a prescription.

**Resistance training.** Not walking. Not yoga. Resistance training — using weights, bands, or bodyweight exercises that challenge muscles to work against a load. Two to three sessions per week is the minimum effective dose. This is the single most protective intervention against sarcopenia, and it works at every age.

**Protein at every meal.** Aim for 25 to 30 grams of protein at each of three daily meals. For vegetarians, this means supplementing dal with paneer, Greek yogurt, eggs (if acceptable), soy, or a protein powder. For non-vegetarians, chicken, fish, and eggs are the most efficient sources.

**Get your parents tested.** Ask their doctor to measure grip strength and walking speed. A simple handgrip dynamometer test costs almost nothing and can flag sarcopenia years before it becomes disabling.

**Reconsider the fast.** If you or your parents are over 50, diabetic or prediabetic, and vegetarian, intermittent fasting may not be the right protocol. The muscle cost may outweigh the metabolic benefit. Talk to a doctor who understands sarcopenia — not just blood sugar.

The generation that raised you on dal-chawal and morning walks did many things right. But the protein gap they lived with for decades is now colliding with a diabetes epidemic that specifically targets muscle tissue. The earlier you intervene, the more muscle — and independence — you can save.
author: Diaspora Desk
